title: Bubble Sort
explanation:
EXPLAINED SIMPLY
Bubble Sort, one step at a time

Imagine moving the heaviest book to the end of a shelf by swapping neighboring books.

Look at two numbers next to each other.
If the left number is bigger, swap them.
Continue to the end. The largest number is now in its final place.
Repeat for the remaining numbers. Stop when a whole pass makes no swaps.
A tiny example

[3, 1, 2] → swap 3 and 1 → [1, 3, 2] → swap 3 and 2 → [1, 2, 3]. The next pass makes no swaps.

When would I use it?

Good for learning comparisons and swaps, or very small lists. Usually too slow for large lists.

What to watch in this animation

Orange marks the current comparison or swap. Green marks positions already settled.
cost: Time: O(n²) average/worst, O(n) best with early exit. Extra space: O(1). Stable.

title: Linear Search
explanation:
EXPLAINED SIMPLY
Linear Search, one step at a time

Find a number the way you search for a name on an unsorted list: check one entry at a time.

Start at index 0, the first position.
Compare the current number with your target.
If they match, return that index and stop.
Otherwise move right. If you reach the end, return −1 to mean not found.
A tiny example

Find 5 in [8, 3, 5]: check 8, then 3, then 5. The result is index 2 because counting starts at 0.

When would I use it?

Works on unsorted data and is simple for short lists. It returns the first match.

What to watch in this animation

Enter a target to try both successful and unsuccessful searches. With an empty target, the lesson picks a value from the list.
cost: Time: O(n) worst, O(1) best. Extra space: O(1).

title: Stack · LIFO
code:
stack = []
for x in [8, 3, 5, 1]:
    stack.append(x)  # push: O(1) amortized
print(stack[-1])  # peek: 1
print(stack.pop()) # pop: 1
print(stack)
explanation:
EXPLAINED SIMPLY
Stack · LIFO, one step at a time

A stack is like a pile of plates: the last plate added is the first one removed.

Push means add an item to the top.
Peek means look at the top without removing it.
Pop means remove the top item.
Only pop or peek when the stack is not empty.
A tiny example

Push 8, then 3, then 5 → [8, 3, 5]. Pop removes 5, leaving [8, 3].

When would I use it?

Useful for undo history, matching brackets, and remembering unfinished work.

What to watch in this animation

This demo uses up to the first eight input values. The rightmost node is the top. It pushes the values, then pops once.
cost: Push/pop: O(1) amortized for Python lists. Peek: O(1). Space: O(n).

title: Breadth-First Search
explanation:
EXPLAINED SIMPLY
Breadth-First Search, one step at a time

Explore nearby places before faraway places, like a ripple spreading out from a stone dropped in water.

Put the starting node in a queue and mark it discovered.
Remove the front node and visit it.
Add each undiscovered neighbor to the back of the queue. Mark it discovered immediately to avoid adding it twice.
Repeat until the queue is empty.
A tiny example

In this graph, start at A → visit B and C → then D, E, and F. The visit order is A, B, C, D, E, F.

When would I use it?

Finds the fewest-edge route from a starting node in an unweighted graph. Store each node’s parent if you also want to reconstruct the route.

What to watch in this animation

The graph is a fixed example. Its connections follow the adjacency lists shown in the Python code; the drawing omits arrowheads. The status shows queue changes.
cost: Time: O(V + E), space: O(V), using adjacency lists.

title: Binary Search Tree
explanation:
EXPLAINED SIMPLY
Binary Search Tree, one step at a time

A binary search tree is a branching number guide: smaller numbers go left and larger numbers go right.

The first inserted value becomes the root.
Compare each new value with the current node.
Go left if smaller, right if larger, and repeat until you find an empty spot.
To read values in order, visit the left subtree, the node itself, then the right subtree.
A tiny example

Insert 8, 3, 10, 6: 8 is the root; 3 goes left; 10 goes right; 6 goes right of 3. An in-order walk gives 3, 6, 8, 10.

When would I use it?

Useful for ordered storage and searching. A balanced tree is fast; a long, one-sided tree can be as slow as scanning a list.

What to watch in this animation

The demo inserts up to seven distinct values. Duplicate values are ignored. The final frame shows the completed tree; it does not animate the in-order walk.
cost: Average search/insert: O(log n) for balanced trees; worst O(n) if skewed. h is tree height.

title: Prefix Sums
code:
def prefix_sums(items):
    result = []
    total = 0
    for value in items:
        total += value
        result.append(total)
    return result

print(prefix_sums([8, 3, 5, 1, 9, 2]))
explanation:
EXPLAINED SIMPLY
Prefix Sums, one step at a time

Keep a running total, like adding each new purchase to your shopping bill.

Start the total at zero.
Add the next number to the total.
Save that total at the same index in a new list.
For a range from l to r, subtract the total before l from the total at r. If l is 0, just use the total at r.
A tiny example

[2, 4, 1, 3] → running totals [2, 6, 7, 10]. Sum at indices 1 through 3 is 10 − 2 = 8, which equals 4 + 1 + 3.

When would I use it?

Useful when you need many range-sum answers for a list whose values stay fixed.

What to watch in this animation

Each processed bar becomes a running total. Unprocessed bars still show the original input values.
cost: Build: O(n), storage: O(n). Range sum [l, r]: prefix[r] minus prefix[l − 1].

title: Maximum Subarray
explanation:
EXPLAINED SIMPLY
Maximum Subarray, one step at a time

Find the best total from a continuous stretch of numbers. At each number, decide whether to extend your stretch or start fresh.

Start with the first number as both the current sum and the best sum.
For each next value, compare that value alone with the current sum plus that value. Keep the larger choice.
Update the best sum if the current sum beats it.
Continue to the end. The selected stretch must contain at least one number.
A tiny example

[-2, 3, -1, 4, -5]: restart at 3, extend to 2, then to 6. The best stretch is [3, -1, 4], with sum 6.

When would I use it?

Useful for finding the most profitable continuous period or strongest continuous signal. If every number is negative, the answer is the largest single number.

What to watch in this animation

The status compares the sum ending here with the best sum seen. Green marks the best stretch so far; the array itself stays unchanged.
cost: Time: O(n); extra space: O(1). Handles all-negative arrays.

title: Dijkstra · Shortest Paths
explanation:
EXPLAINED SIMPLY
Dijkstra · Shortest Paths, one step at a time

Imagine finding the cheapest travel costs from your home. Always finish the cheapest unfinished destination next.

Give A distance 0 and all other vertices distance infinity.
Choose the unfinished vertex with the smallest distance. Its distance is final because edge weights are nonnegative.
For each neighbor, compare its current distance with the cost of going through this vertex. Keep the cheaper route.
Repeat until no reachable unfinished vertices remain.
A tiny example

A→B costs 4, A→C costs 2, and C→B costs 1. Going through C costs 3, so B improves from 4 to 3.

When would I use it?

Road routing and other shortest-path problems with nonnegative edge weights. Negative weights require a different algorithm.

What to watch in this animation

The fixed undirected graph shows edge weights. The table records the best distances from A; green vertices have final distances.
cost: This demo scans vertices: O(V² + E) time, O(V) working space. A priority queue implementation can improve sparse-graph performance.

title: Longest Increasing Subsequence
explanation:
EXPLAINED SIMPLY
Longest Increasing Subsequence, one step at a time

Pick numbers from left to right so each chosen number is bigger than the last. You may skip numbers, but cannot reorder them.

Give every index a starting length of 1: a single number is already an increasing subsequence.
For each index i, inspect earlier indices j.
If value[j] is smaller than value[i], try extending the best subsequence ending at j. Keep the longest option and remember its previous index.
Find the largest length and follow previous indices backward to recover one answer.
A tiny example

In [3, 1, 2, 5, 4], one longest increasing subsequence is [1, 2, 5], with length 3. [1, 2, 4] is equally valid.

When would I use it?

Finding ordered trends when skipped values are allowed. Unlike maximum subarray, the chosen positions need not be next to each other.

What to watch in this animation

The table gives the longest length ending at each index. Highlighted input cells in the final frame show one valid longest subsequence.
cost: Time: O(n²), space: O(n) for lengths and parent pointers. Equal values do not extend a strictly increasing sequence.

title: KMP · Pattern Matching
explanation:
EXPLAINED SIMPLY
KMP · Pattern Matching, one step at a time

When a partial match fails, reuse what you already know instead of starting the whole comparison again.

Build an LPS table for the pattern: each entry stores the longest proper prefix that is also a suffix of the pattern ending there. Proper means shorter than the whole part.
Compare the text and pattern from left to right. On a match, move both positions forward.
On a mismatch after some matches, set the pattern position to the previous LPS value. Keep the text position unchanged.
If the whole pattern matches, return its starting index. If the text ends first, return −1.
A tiny example

For pattern ABAB, the LPS table is [0, 0, 1, 2]. In text ABACABAB, a mismatch after ABA falls back to a known prefix, and the full pattern is found at index 4.

When would I use it?

Searching text efficiently, especially when repeated prefixes cause naive matching to redo comparisons.

What to watch in this animation

Use the Text and Pattern controls. Matching is case-sensitive. Indices count Unicode code points; spaces are meaningful. The LPS table is built before text scanning.
cost: Time: O(n + m), space: O(m) for the prefix table. This demo returns the first match, or −1.

title: Z Algorithm · Pattern Search
explanation:
EXPLAINED SIMPLY
Z Algorithm · Pattern Search, one step at a time

Measure how much of the beginning repeats at every position. Put the pattern first so those measurements reveal matches.

Join pattern, a unique separator, and text. The separator cannot match any character.
Keep a reusable interval, called the Z box, where characters already match the beginning.
Use the box to avoid rechecking known matches, then extend it when needed.
Any text position whose Z value reaches the pattern length is a match.
A tiny example

Text ABABABA and pattern ABA have matches at indices [0, 2, 4]. Overlapping matches count.

When would I use it?

Find every occurrence of one pattern, or identify repeated prefixes.

What to watch in this animation

The separator is an internal token, so even text containing ⟂ is safe. Z[0] is defined as 0 here.
cost: O(n + m) algorithm time. n = text length; m = second-input length. For dictionary lessons, S = total word characters and p = prefix length. The separator is an internal token, so even text containing ⟂ is safe. Z[0] is defined as 0 here. Animation snapshots add storage and rendering work beyond algorithm-only complexity.

title: Trie · Prefix Autocomplete
explanation:
EXPLAINED SIMPLY
Trie · Prefix Autocomplete, one step at a time

Store words as paths of characters. A shared beginning is stored once, so you can jump straight to a prefix’s suggestions.

Insert each word one character at a time, reusing existing branches.
Mark the end of each full word.
Follow the characters of the requested prefix.
Walk below that node and collect complete words.
A tiny example

Prefix ca in [car, card, care, cat, dog] returns car, card, care, cat.

When would I use it?

Autocomplete and prefix lookup over a dictionary.

What to watch in this animation

Text is the prefix here. An empty prefix returns all words. Duplicate words are removed. The demo sorts suggestions, adding O(k log k) string comparisons for k results; storing displayed prefixes also adds trace overhead.
cost: O(S + p + output) algorithm time. n = text length; m = second-input length. For dictionary lessons, S = total word characters and p = prefix length. Text is the prefix here. An empty prefix returns all words. Duplicate words are removed. The demo sorts suggestions, adding O(k log k) string comparisons for k results; storing displayed prefixes also adds trace overhead. Animation snapshots add storage and rendering work beyond algorithm-only complexity.

title: Manacher · Longest Palindrome
explanation:
EXPLAINED SIMPLY
Manacher · Longest Palindrome, one step at a time

A palindrome reads the same in both directions. Reuse mirror information inside a known palindrome instead of expanding every center from scratch.

Process odd-length and even-length centers separately.
If a center lies inside the current palindrome, borrow the safe radius from its mirror.
Expand only beyond the portion already known to match.
Keep the rightmost palindrome boundary and the longest answer seen.
A tiny example

babad contains bab and aba, each length 3. This lesson returns bab. cbbd returns bb.

When would I use it?

Finding the longest continuous palindrome in linear time.

What to watch in this animation

Odd radii include the center. Even radii use a center immediately before an index. Algorithm storage is O(n); snapshots add overhead.
cost: O(n) algorithm time. n = text length; m = second-input length. For dictionary lessons, S = total word characters and p = prefix length. Odd radii include the center. Even radii use a center immediately before an index. Algorithm storage is O(n); snapshots add overhead. Animation snapshots add storage and rendering work beyond algorithm-only complexity.

title: Longest Common Subsequence
explanation:
EXPLAINED SIMPLY
Longest Common Subsequence, one step at a time

Find a sequence of characters appearing in both strings in the same order. You may skip characters.

Create a table for every pair of prefix lengths, including empty prefixes.
If the last characters match, extend the diagonal answer by one.
Otherwise keep the larger answer from removing one character from either prefix.
Walk backward through the table to recover one longest subsequence.
A tiny example

ABC and AC have common subsequence AC of length 2. The B is skipped.

When would I use it?

Comparing revisions and measuring ordered similarity.

What to watch in this animation

Rows are text prefixes; columns are second-string prefixes. This full-table version uses O(nm) space. Ties can produce different valid answers.
cost: O(nm) algorithm time. n = text length; m = second-input length. For dictionary lessons, S = total word characters and p = prefix length. Rows are text prefixes; columns are second-string prefixes. This full-table version uses O(nm) space. Ties can produce different valid answers. Animation snapshots add storage and rendering work beyond algorithm-only complexity.

title: Minimum Window Substring
explanation:
EXPLAINED SIMPLY
Minimum Window Substring, one step at a time

Find the smallest continuous window containing all requested characters, including duplicate requirements.

Count how many of each required character you need.
Expand the right end and update counts until every requirement is met.
Record the window, then move its left end right while it remains valid.
Continue expanding and shrinking, remembering the shortest valid window.
A tiny example

For ADOBECODEBANC and ABC, the smallest valid window is BANC.

When would I use it?

Finding a compact text span containing a required multiset of characters.

What to watch in this animation

The order of required characters does not matter, but their counts do. An impossible requirement or empty requirement returns an empty string. Each boundary moves only forward; auxiliary counts use O(n + m) space here.
cost: O(n + m) algorithm time. n = text length; m = second-input length. For dictionary lessons, S = total word characters and p = prefix length. The order of required characters does not matter, but their counts do. An impossible requirement or empty requirement returns an empty string. Each boundary moves only forward; auxiliary counts use O(n + m) space here. Animation snapshots add storage and rendering work beyond algorithm-only complexity.

title: Literal Substring Search
code:
# Literal Substring Search
# Python re syntax applies; JavaScript regex Unicode rules can differ.
"""Shared reference for 30 regex recipes. Python re syntax applies.

Browser lessons use JavaScript regex syntax. The supplied ASCII examples agree;
arbitrary patterns, Unicode classes, and case folding may differ between engines.
This Python helper does not impose a worker timeout: only run trusted patterns.
"""
import re


def regex_recipe(text, pattern, mode='matches', flags='', replacement=''):
    """Match, validate, split, or replace using explicit code-point spans.

    Replacement syntax is $1 through $9 and $$, matching the teaching UI.
    Split keeps empty pieces without inserting captured separators. Empty
    matches advance one code point; nonempty matches are non-overlapping.
    """
    if mode not in {'matches', 'validate', 'split', 'replace'}:
        raise ValueError('Unknown regex operation')
    if any(flag not in 'ims' for flag in flags) or len(set(flags)) != len(flags):
        raise ValueError('Flags may contain i, m, and s once each')
    options = 0
    for flag in flags:
        options |= {'i': re.IGNORECASE, 'm': re.MULTILINE, 's': re.DOTALL}[flag]
    expression = re.compile(pattern, options)
    if mode == 'validate':
        return expression.fullmatch(text) is not None
    matches, pieces, cursor, position = [], [], 0, 0
    while position <= len(text):
        match = expression.search(text, position)
        if match is None:
            break
        matches.append({'match': match.group(0), 'start': match.start(),
                        'end': match.end(), 'groups': list(match.groups())})
        if mode == 'split':
            pieces.append(text[cursor:match.start()])
            cursor = match.end()
        elif mode == 'replace':
            def expand(token):
                key = token.group(1)
                if key == '$':
                    return '$'
                index = int(key)
                return (match.group(index) or '') if index <= expression.groups else '$' + key
            pieces.extend([text[cursor:match.start()], re.sub(r'\$(\$|[1-9])', expand, replacement)])
            cursor = match.end()
        position = match.end() + (match.start() == match.end())
    if mode in {'split', 'replace'}:
        pieces.append(text[cursor:])
        return pieces if mode == 'split' else ''.join(pieces)
    return matches


print(regex_recipe("The cat saw another cat.", "cat", "matches", "", ""))
explanation:
EXPLAINED SIMPLY
Literal Substring Search, one step at a time

Read a literal pattern as the exact characters to find.

cat has no special regex characters: it searches for those three letters together.
Find the next leftmost match, starting after the previous match.
Record its text, half-open start/end span, and capture groups.
Continue until no matches remain; an empty match advances by one code point.
A tiny example

Two cat matches start at indices 4 and 20.

When would I use it?

Finding a fixed fragment. Escape special characters such as . when they should be literal.

What to watch in this animation

The animation shows match-level results, not hidden engine backtracking. Spans are [start, end), indexed by Unicode code points. Regex runtime depends on the pattern and may be exponential. Evaluation runs in a worker that is stopped after 1.5 seconds. Python examples use Python re; dialect and Unicode class rules differ from JavaScript.

import re


def regex_recipe(text, pattern, mode='matches', flags='', replacement=''):
    """Match, validate, split, or replace using explicit code-point spans.

    Replacement syntax is $1 through $9 and $$, matching the teaching UI.
    Split keeps empty pieces without inserting captured separators. Empty
    matches advance one code point; nonempty matches are non-overlapping.
    """
    if mode not in {'matches', 'validate', 'split', 'replace'}:
        raise ValueError('Unknown regex operation')
    if any(flag not in 'ims' for flag in flags) or len(set(flags)) != len(flags):
        raise ValueError('Flags may contain i, m, and s once each')
    options = 0
    for flag in flags:
        options |= {'i': re.IGNORECASE, 'm': re.MULTILINE, 's': re.DOTALL}[flag]
    expression = re.compile(pattern, options)
    if mode == 'validate':
        return expression.fullmatch(text) is not None
    matches, pieces, cursor, position = [], [], 0, 0
    while position <= len(text):
        match = expression.search(text, position)
        if match is None:
            break
        matches.append({'match': match.group(0), 'start': match.start(),
                        'end': match.end(), 'groups': list(match.groups())})
        if mode == 'split':
            pieces.append(text[cursor:match.start()])
            cursor = match.end()
        elif mode == 'replace':
            def expand(token):
                key = token.group(1)
                if key == '$':
                    return '$'
                index = int(key)
                return (match.group(index) or '') if index <= expression.groups else '$' + key
            pieces.extend([text[cursor:match.start()], re.sub(r'\$(\$|[1-9])', expand, replacement)])
            cursor = match.end()
        position = match.end() + (match.start() == match.end())
    if mode in {'split', 'replace'}:
        pieces.append(text[cursor:])
        return pieces if mode == 'split' else ''.join(pieces)
    return matches

Two Sum · Complement Hash Map, one step at a time

Remember earlier values so each new number can ask whether its missing partner has already appeared.

For [2,7,11,15] and target 9, 2 needs 7; at index 1, earlier 2 completes the pair [0,1].

title: Product Except Self · Prefix/Suffix
code:
from collections import Counter, deque
import heapq


def product_except_self(nums):
    result, prefix, suffix = [1] * len(nums), 1, 1
    for i, value in enumerate(nums):
        result[i] = prefix
        prefix *= value
    for i in range(len(nums) - 1, -1, -1):
        result[i] *= suffix
        suffix *= nums[i]
    return result

print(product_except_self(nums=[1, 2, 3, 4]))
explanation:
EXPLAINED SIMPLY

At each position, multiply everything before it by everything after it, without dividing.

Walk left to right, storing the product strictly before each index.
Walk right to left with a running product strictly after each index.
Multiply the two contributions at that index.
Keep zeros as ordinary factors; division is never needed.
A tiny example

[1,2,3,4] produces [24,12,8,6]. With [2,0,4], the result is [0,8,0].

Computing per-position aggregates while excluding the current element.

title: Meeting Rooms II · End-Time Heap
code:
from collections import Counter, deque
import heapq


def meeting_rooms(intervals):
    active, best = [], 0
    for start, end in sorted(intervals):
        while active and active[0] <= start:
            heapq.heappop(active)
        heapq.heappush(active, end)
        best = max(best, len(active))
    return best

print(meeting_rooms(intervals=[[0, 30], [5, 10], [15, 20]]))

EXPLAINED SIMPLY
Meeting Rooms II · End-Time Heap, one step at a time

Reuse a room as soon as its earliest-ending meeting finishes; peak simultaneous meetings determine room demand.

Sort meetings by start time.
Remove every active end time no later than the next start.
Add the new meeting end to a min heap.
Record the largest number of active meetings.
A tiny example

[[0,30],[5,10],[15,20]] needs 2 rooms. A meeting ending at 10 can share a room with one starting at 10.

When would I use it?

Resource allocation and maximum overlap in time intervals.

Keep unresolved indices on a stack until a larger value arrives to answer them.

from collections import Counter, deque
import heapq


def house_robber(nums):
    previous_two = previous_one = 0
    for value in nums:
        previous_two, previous_one = previous_one, max(previous_one, previous_two + value)
    return previous_one

At each house, either skip it or take it together with the best reward ending before its neighbor.

Start with reward 0 for empty prefixes.
Compare previous best with best two houses back plus this house’s value.
Keep the better option and roll the two states forward.
Return the best reward; choosing no house is allowed.
A tiny example

[2,7,9,3,1] yields 12 by taking values 2,9,1. Adjacent houses cannot both be selected.

Selection problems with local incompatibility constraints.

title: Subsets · Backtracking
code:
from collections import Counter, deque
import heapq


def subsets(nums):
    result, path = [], []
    def visit(start):
        result.append(path.copy())
        for i in range(start, len(nums)):
            path.append(nums[i])
            visit(i + 1)
            path.pop()
    visit(0)
    return result

print(subsets(nums=[1, 2, 3]))

EXPLAINED SIMPLY
Subsets · Backtracking, one step at a time

Build every subset by choosing only indices after the last selected one.

Record the current partial selection as a valid subset.
Choose each later index in turn.
Recurse starting after that chosen index.
Undo the choice before exploring the next branch.
A tiny example

[1,2] produces [], [1], [1,2], and [2]. The empty subset is included.

When would I use it?

Generating a power set while maintaining increasing chosen indices.
